segments.say: Here's a pattern that catches many capable, well paid people by surprise. They get a raise. Then another. Their income grows a lot over the years. And yet, somehow, they don't feel richer. They still live close to the edge of their income. Saving still feels hard. Where did all the extra money go?

Often, the answer is something called lifestyle creep, or lifestyle inflation. As income rises, spending rises with it. A slightly nicer flat. A slightly better car. Eating out a little more often. More expensive holidays. Each upgrade feels small and reasonable. But together, they can absorb almost all of the extra income.

Remember the hedonic treadmill from our last episode. We adapt quickly to improvements. The nicer flat becomes normal within months. So the upgrade stops feeling like an upgrade, and we start looking for the next one. Meanwhile, the higher cost stays forever. The pleasure fades, but the bill remains.

Comparison plays a role as well. As we earn more, we often move into new circles, with colleagues and friends who spend more. What feels normal shifts upward. Remember spending to be seen. Our reference points rise with our income, so we keep feeling that we're just keeping up.

Intelligent, high earning people are not protected from this. In fact, they may be especially exposed, because their incomes rise faster, and because their social circles often have high spending norms. A doctor, lawyer or engineer can earn a very good income, and still feel financially stretched.

One simple, widely recommended approach is to decide in advance what happens to future raises. Remember Save More Tomorrow, where people committed to saving part of their future pay increases. You might decide, for example, that half of every raise goes to savings, and half to enjoying life more. That way, your lifestyle still improves, but not by the full amount.

Another approach is to make upgrades deliberate, rather than automatic. When you consider a lifestyle upgrade, ask, will this still make me happier in six months? Or will it become normal, while the cost stays? Upgrades that bring lasting value, like more time, better health or shared experiences, may be worth more than ones that quickly fade.

Some people find it helpful to think about the gap between income and spending as freedom. Every euro you don't spend on something you'll quickly adapt to is a euro that can buy future security, flexibility, or the ability to say no to a job you don't like. That freedom is a kind of wealth that doesn't show, but feels wonderful.

This doesn't mean you shouldn't enjoy rising income. Of course you should. Enjoy the good things. The point is simply to choose them consciously, so that your money grows your life, rather than just your costs. A little restraint today can turn into a lot of calm tomorrow.

So here's what lifestyle creep teaches us. Spending tends to rise along with income. We adapt to upgrades quickly, but their costs remain. Deciding in advance what happens to future raises can protect our savings. And making upgrades deliberate, rather than automatic, helps money grow our lives, not just our costs.

show.title: The quiet creep
items: Decide in advance what happens to raises

segments.say: We're nearly at the end of our journey now. Before we slow down for the night, let's take one last look back at what we've learned about why smart people make bad money decisions, and how we can be a little kinder and wiser with our own.
